title: Blockbuster Passed on Netflix for $50M. Would You?
titleAlternatives: Would You Have Bought Netflix for $50 Million?
Netflix Lost More Than Its Price. Would You Buy It?
The Blockbuster CEO Who Passed on Netflix
From 9,094 Stores to One: Blockbuster's $50M No
description:
In 2000, a money-losing start-up that mailed DVDs to people's homes named its price: $50 million. The company across the table had thousands of stores and close to $5 billion in yearly revenue. Blockbuster did not buy Netflix.

Today Netflix is worth hundreds of billions of dollars, and Blockbuster is down to one franchised store in Bend, Oregon. But the story is more complicated than the legend. Three people remember that meeting in Dallas in three different ways. Sit in John Antioco's chair and decide for yourself.

Would you have signed? Tell us in the comments.

pinnedComment: Netflix lost more in 2000 than the $50M it was asking, while Blockbuster's own stores were still growing. Honest answer: would you have signed?

shorts.hook: Fifty million dollars was the price on a money-losing start-up that mailed DVDs to people's homes.
shorts.question: Netflix lost more than $50 million that year, and your own stores are still growing. Would you sign?
shorts.reveal: Blockbuster said no. Today Netflix is worth hundreds of billions, and Blockbuster has one franchised store left, in Bend, Oregon.

shorts.hook: One of the most famous rejections in business history rests on three memories that don't match.
shorts.question: Randolph says Blockbuster laughed them out of the room. Antioco says there were never serious talks. Who do you believe?
shorts.reveal: Everyone agrees on three things: a meeting in Dallas, a $50 million number, and no deal. Even Hastings reportedly recalls more curiosity than a serious pitch.
